slides.title: Chapter 8: Riemannian Submanifolds
slides.notes: Frame the chapter as the place where the curvature machinery from chapter seven meets concrete surfaces. The central question is how the geometry an embedded submanifold inherits from its ambient space splits cleanly into a tangential intrinsic part and a normal extrinsic part. Tell the audience that today's vocabulary, especially the second fundamental form, will let them read off curvature from how a surface bends inside a larger manifold.

slides.title: Tangential and Normal: Splitting the Ambient Connection
slides.notes: Start with the geometric picture: a submanifold sits inside a larger Riemannian manifold, and at every point of the submanifold the ambient tangent space splits orthogonally into the tangent and normal directions. Stress that the induced metric is just the restriction of the ambient metric to tangent vectors. The whole chapter exploits this decomposition repeatedly, so make sure students see the picture before any formulas appear.

slides.title: The Gauss Formula: Induced Connection Plus II
slides.notes: The Gauss formula is the central organizing identity of the chapter. Walk through why the tangential part of the ambient covariant derivative deserves to be called the Levi-Civita connection of the induced metric: it is torsion free and metric compatible, so uniqueness forces the identification. Emphasize that the normal part is not a new connection but a tensor, the second fundamental form, which measures how Y leaves the submanifold as one moves in the direction X.

slides.title: The Second Fundamental Form II(X,Y)
slides.notes: Make sure students see two facts about the second fundamental form. First, it depends only on the pointwise values of the inputs, so it is genuinely a tensor field. Second, it is symmetric, which is the price the ambient connection pays for being torsion free. The geometric reading is that II records the failure of a tangent vector field to stay parallel to the submanifold under ambient transport, encoded as a vector in the normal bundle.

slides.title: The Weingarten Equation and the Shape Operator
slides.notes: Present the Weingarten equation as the dual viewpoint to the Gauss formula. Instead of differentiating tangent vector fields and reading off the normal part, we differentiate a normal field and read off the tangential part. The minus sign comes from differentiating the constraint that N is orthogonal to Y. The payoff is the shape operator, a self adjoint endomorphism of the tangent space whose eigenvalues will become the principal curvatures.

slides.title: The Gauss Equation: Ambient Curvature Meets Intrinsic Curvature
slides.notes: The Gauss equation is the headline identity of the chapter. Spell out that the left side is a purely intrinsic quantity, the curvature of the induced metric; the first term on the right is the restriction of the ambient curvature; and the remaining terms are quadratic in the second fundamental form. The slide flags the connection to Gauss's theorema egregium: in flat ambient space, intrinsic curvature is built entirely from II, which is exactly the statement that Gaussian curvature is intrinsic.

slides.title: The Codazzi Equation: How II Differentiates
slides.notes: Frame Codazzi as the compatibility condition that II is not free to be any symmetric tensor field; it must satisfy a differential constraint coming from the ambient curvature. Introduce the normal connection briefly: it is just the normal projection of the ambient connection applied to normal fields. The headline consequence is that in a constant-curvature ambient space, II is a Codazzi tensor, meaning its covariant derivative is symmetric in all three lower slots.

slides.title: Euclidean Hypersurfaces: Principal and Mean Curvature
slides.notes: Specialize to codimension one. With a chosen unit normal, the second fundamental form is recorded by a single symmetric bilinear form whose self-adjoint counterpart is the shape operator. Its eigenvalues are the classical principal curvatures, and their average is the mean curvature. Emphasize that for a hypersurface in Euclidean space the Gauss equation reduces to the elegant statement that the sectional curvature in a principal plane is the product of principal curvatures, the higher-dimensional analogue of Gauss's curvature formula for surfaces.

slides.title: Sectional Curvature of a Submanifold
slides.notes: This slide makes the Gauss equation operational. The intrinsic sectional curvature of a two-plane is the ambient sectional curvature of the same plane plus a correction built from the second fundamental form. The correction is nonnegative when II is definite on the plane and negative when II is saddle-like. Hand-wave this against students' mental images of a sphere and a saddle sitting in Euclidean space, and connect the formula to the Euclidean-hypersurface case from the previous slide.

slides.title: Recap: The Submanifold Toolkit
slides.notes: Close by tying the slides together into a single procedure. Given any embedded submanifold, the workflow is: split the ambient connection, identify the induced connection and the second fundamental form, then use Gauss and Codazzi to translate between ambient and intrinsic curvature data. The diagnostic question on the slide is the test the chapter equips students to pass: if they can carry out the computation on a sphere, a graph, or a constant-mean-curvature surface, the toolkit has been internalized.
